person.name: Daniel (Dani) Idemudia
person.tagline: I make things you can hold: prints, prototypes and machines.
person.intro: A collection of what I've designed, printed and built: product prototypes for two startup teams, statues sculpted with AI and finished by hand in the slicer, NFC hardware for an iPhone app, and the PCs I've built from parts. Every 3D project links the real print to the file it came from, and the files are free to download.

projects.title: The Beaver Dam NFC roundel
projects.summary: A printed beaver coin with an NFC tag sealed inside. Tap it with your phone to unlock the apps you blocked.

cover.alt: White 3D-printed round coin with a raised beaver face

story: The Beaver Dam is an iPhone focus app I'm building with a team. You lock distracting apps with Screen Time, and the only everyday way to unlock them is to physically tap a beaver token with your phone. The token has to sit on a desk or a keychain and still read on the first tap, every time.

My first prototype used a cheap tag inside a printed block. It often missed the first tap and sometimes died completely. So I wrote a hardware brief for the team and treated the token as an experiment: change one variable at a time (tag size, how much plastic sits over it, where it lines up with the phone's antenna, how well it's protected) and print a family of variants to test.

The designs are parametric. Wall thickness, tag-pocket diameter and tag depth are numbers at the top of the file, so each test print changes exactly one thing. The current design is a 100 mm roundel with a beaver in relief. The tag drops into a pocket and a printed cap seals it in, and a 70 mm version uses the same idea in a smaller size.
highlights: 3 early concepts (A, B, C), then 100 mm and 70 mm roundels
Separate 30 mm cap seals the tag in, so it can't peel off or shift
Edge slot shows the tag pocket. A full build plate prints several at once
Pairs with a working SwiftUI app that reads the tag to end a focus session

projects.title: Powertown Powerblock scale model
projects.summary: A desk-sized model of an energy-storage unit with a hinged door and five battery modules that slide out.
story: Powertown installs Powerblocks, on-site battery storage that charges when power is cheap and runs the building when it's expensive, at no cost to local businesses, schools and town buildings. Most people have never seen one, so the team needed something they could put on a table and open.

I modeled a one-piece shell with rails for five black battery modules, a front door on a printed hinge, and a faceplate with the rating and logo in relief. The inside of the door has raised blocks standing in for the inverter, controller and wiring, so opening it shows what's inside the real thing.

It went through four versions. v1 was a simple block, v2 added the door, v3 split the parts by color, and v4 added the textured faceplate and vent grille. I printed it in white for the first prototype (125 kW) and then in black for the presentation version (130 kW).
highlights: 4 design versions, from a simple block to a working door and slide-out modules
Multi-part assembly: shell, hinged door, faceplate, 5 modules
Printed hinge with no hardware. The modules slide on printed rails
Used as a hands-on prop in community and college pitches

projects.title: "Dani the King" winged statue
projects.summary: A 20 cm winged self-portrait bust on an engraved two-tier base, from a single photo to a finished print.
story: I turned a photo of myself into a 3D bust with Meshy AI, then did the real work by hand. I cleaned up the mesh, added wings and a raised fist, and built a two-tier pedestal with engraved lettering.

The hard part was the wings. They're thin, overhang a lot and fan out away from the body, so I used tree supports that branch up from the base without touching the face. The second photo shows the print fresh off the plate with the supports still on, and the first shows it cleaned up.
highlights: About 23 × 16 × 20 cm, printed in one piece
Tree supports for long, thin overhanging wings
Engraved base lettering
Also made an 18 cm desk version

projects.title: Anime birthday statue for Koko
projects.summary: A birthday diorama of me and a friend in an anime finishing pose, assembled and engraved with a Python script.
story: For my friend Koko's birthday I made a diorama of the two of us. I generated each figure with AI, then wrote a Python build script (trimesh + manifold3d) that scales, rotates and places the figures, and generates the pedestal and engraved text. Changing the layout means changing a number and running the script again.

The first version is a clean plinth that says HAPPY BIRTHDAY KOKO. The anime version adds a starburst backdrop, a flame aura and a scarf on my figure, swords and a headband on Koko's, and a cracked rock base. I also generated five sword poses to pick the strongest silhouette, and printed a 50 mm test figure to check detail at small scale.
highlights: Pedestal, text and layout generated from code, with settings at the top of the script
2 versions: a clean plinth and an anime diorama with an aura backdrop
5 pose variants compared side by side before committing
50 mm test print to check detail at small scale

projects.title: Bike-shaped NFC tags
projects.summary: A small run of bicycle-shaped NFC tags. One wheel holds the tag and the other carries engraved text.
story: A flat bicycle silhouette where the back wheel is a shallow pocket sized for a round NFC sticker and the front wheel carries engraved text. I iterated the outline across four versions to get the thin frame tubes strong enough, then printed a batch.

This was my first NFC-in-a-print project, and it's where I learned what a tag needs: a pocket with the right depth so the phone reads it, and a frame thick enough not to snap. That carried straight into the Beaver Dam roundel.
highlights: Wheel pocket sized for a round NFC inlay
4 outline versions, then a batch print
Engraved text in the opposite wheel

projects.title: Powertown desk figure kit
projects.summary: A team nameplate system: one OpenSCAD template, a logo piece that presses in, and a one-page guide so anyone can make their own.
story: I designed desk figures for the Powertown team: a navy base with the person's name and title, and the Powertown logo mark pressed into a pocket on top.

Instead of modeling each plate by hand, I wrote the base as an OpenSCAD template and wrote instructions for teammates: upload the .scad to Claude, ask it to change only the name and title, then print with no supports at 0.2 mm layers. A new team member can get a nameplate without me.
highlights: One parametric template makes every nameplate
Logo mark press-fits into the base, no supports needed
Written handoff guide so teammates can make their own

projects.title: Bust and medallion series
projects.summary: One AI-generated self-portrait, printed again and again: a bust lineup, a pedestal bust and a wall medallion.
story: Before the winged statue I printed the same bust several times to learn what holds up at small sizes, like curly hair, eye detail and thin arms. The lineup photo shows those prints side by side on cork-backed bases.
From the same model I also made a bust on a pedestal and a 100 mm wall medallion in relief, which turns a 3D bust into something nearly flat that hangs on a wall.
highlights: 5-print lineup comparing detail at small scale
Same model turned into a relief medallion
Cork-backed bases for desk use

projects.title: Nico portrait bust
projects.summary: A 50 mm head-and-shoulders portrait with curly hair, a crew-neck tee and wired earbuds trailing from the ears.
story: A small portrait bust: curly hair, eyes looking down, a crew-neck T-shirt, and a pair of wired earbuds running from the ears down over the shirt.
At this size the challenge is fine detail: the hair texture and the thin, free-hanging earbud cords.
highlights: Hair texture and free-hanging earbud cords as fine-detail tests

projects.title: PC builds
projects.summary: Three computers built or upgraded from parts: a white Ryzen build, a black NZXT RGB build, and a Dell mini-PC storage upgrade.
story: White build: a Ryzen 5 5600 on an ASRock B550 Phantom Gaming 4/ac in a white Corsair case, with an ID-Cooling tower cooler, white RAM, a 1 TB Silicon Power NVMe drive, an M.2 Wi-Fi card, an EVGA SuperNOVA power supply and an NVIDIA RTX Founders Edition card. I planned the cable routing and wired the fans through a Corsair RGB/fan hub.
Black build: an NZXT case with an ASUS TUF Gaming board, T-Force Delta RGB memory, a Sapphire Radeon card and a Ryzen with the stock AMD cooler, all lit purple through the mesh top.
Upgrade: I opened a Dell mini PC and moved it from a 240 GB SATA SSD to a 1 TB NVMe drive. I also have a white ASUS Dual RTX card ready for the next upgrade.
highlights: Full builds from bare parts: CPU, cooler, RAM, NVMe, Wi-Fi card, PSU, GPU
Front-panel USB, fan hub and RGB wiring
Storage upgrade on a compact business PC

projects.title: Small experiments
projects.summary: Quick prints that taught me something: a fit test for a curtain-ring clip, and a horse diorama on a sculpted base.
story: The curtain ring is a fit test for a functional clip, where the gap and the arm thickness have to be right on the first print or it snaps or falls off. The horse diorama started as an AI-generated horse that I placed on a round meadow base with a fence. The second version is the one in the files.
highlights: Functional fit test: clip tolerance
Character on a sculpted scene base
